::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## What this lesson is for

This is where the data starts answering real questions: *What is the total catch at each district? Which
gear brings in the most? How many trips were recorded last month?*

All of these are **"add it up by group"** questions. This lesson shows you how, with two commands.
Press **Run** on each box. Remember: **you cannot break anything.**
:::

## First, one question from last time

Bring back one thing from the last lesson before we add to it. A wrong answer costs nothing.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof recall_filter = Inputs.radio(
  ["distinct()", "filter()", "select()"],
  { label: "Which command keeps only some of the rows?" }
)
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
html`${
  // `== null` on purpose: Inputs.radio starts at null, not undefined, when nothing is picked.
  recall_filter == null
    ? '<div class="alert alert-light py-2">Pick an answer above.</div>'
    : recall_filter === "filter()"
      ? '<div class="alert alert-success py-2"><strong>Yes.</strong> <code>filter()</code> keeps rows. <code>select()</code> keeps columns, and <code>distinct()</code> lists the values in a column once each.</div>'
      : '<div class="alert alert-warning py-2"><strong>Have another look.</strong> Rows go across, and <code>filter()</code> is the one that keeps only some of them. <code>select()</code> keeps <em>columns</em>, and <code>distinct()</code> lists the values in a column once each.</div>'
}`
```

## Before we start

{{< include _before-we-start.qmd >}}

## One number for your whole table

**`summarise()`** turns a whole column into a single answer. To add up all the weights, you give the
answer a name (`total_kg`) and tell R to `sum` the `catch_kg` column. Press **Run**:

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
example |>
  summarise(total_kg = sum(catch_kg))
```

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**What you should see:** one row with **`total_kg = 34`**. That is the weight of all five catches added
together (12 + 5 + 3 + 8 + 6). The part `total_kg =` is just the **name** you chose for the answer.
:::

You can ask for more than one answer at a time. **`n()`** counts the rows. Press **Run**:

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
example |>
  summarise(total_kg = sum(catch_kg), number_of_catches = n())
```

## A number for each group

A single total for everything is rarely what you want. Usually you want **one total per district**, or per
gear, or per month. That is what **`group_by()`** is for: you tell R which column to group on, and then
`summarise()` gives you **one answer for each group**.

**Have a guess first.** The `example` table has **5 rows**, in two districts: Shimoni and Vanga.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof predict_group = Inputs.radio(
  ["5 rows — one for each catch", "2 rows — one for each district", "1 row — one grand total"],
  { label: "How many rows will the answer have?" }
)
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
html`${
  // `== null` on purpose: Inputs.radio starts at null, not undefined, when nothing is picked.
  predict_group == null
    ? '<div class="alert alert-light py-2">Pick an answer above, then press Run below to check it.</div>'
    : predict_group === "2 rows — one for each district"
      ? '<div class="alert alert-success py-2"><strong>Yes — 2 rows.</strong> This is the whole idea of grouping: <strong>one row of answer for each group</strong>. Two districts, so two rows.</div>'
      : '<div class="alert alert-warning py-2"><strong>Have another look.</strong> Grouping gives you <strong>one row of answer per group</strong>. So ask yourself: how many different districts are there? A wrong guess here is a useful one — this is the step people find hardest.</div>'
}`
```

Now press **Run**:

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
example |>
  group_by(gaul_2_name) |>
  summarise(total_kg = sum(catch_kg))
```

Read it as: *take the example, **group by** district, **then** add up the weight in each group.* Here is
what that does to the rows:

```{=html}
<div class="diagram diagram-flow">
<table class="table">
  <thead><tr><th>gaul_2_name</th><th>catch_kg</th></tr></thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr class="grp-a"><td>Shimoni</td><td>12</td></tr>
    <tr class="grp-a"><td>Shimoni</td><td>5</td></tr>
    <tr class="grp-a"><td>Shimoni</td><td>3</td></tr>
    <tr class="grp-b"><td>Vanga</td><td>8</td></tr>
    <tr class="grp-b"><td>Vanga</td><td>6</td></tr>
  </tbody>
</table>
<div class="arrow">&#8594;</div>
<table class="table">
  <thead><tr><th>gaul_2_name</th><th>total_kg</th></tr></thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr class="grp-a"><td>Shimoni</td><td>20</td></tr>
    <tr class="grp-b"><td>Vanga</td><td>14</td></tr>
  </tbody>
</table>
</div>
```
[Each district's rows collapse into one total. Shimoni's three rows (12 + 5 + 3) become **20**. Vanga's
two (8 + 6) become **14**.]{.diagram-caption}

## More than one summary, on any column

You can group by **any** column, and ask for several summaries at once. **`mean()`** gives the average.
This groups by the kind of fish and shows the total, the average, and the count for each:

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
example |>
  group_by(catch_taxon) |>
  summarise(
    total_kg   = sum(catch_kg),
    average_kg = mean(catch_kg),
    number     = n()
  )
```

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**What you should see:** one row for each kind of fish: **species 1**, **species 2** and **species 3**.
Each row has its total weight, its average weight, and how many catches there were.
:::

## Now your own data

Let's total the catch **per district** in your real data.

Real records sometimes have a **missing** weight. Adding `na.rm = TRUE` tells R to skip those, so you
still get an answer. Press **Run**:

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
landings |>
  group_by(gaul_2_name) |>
  summarise(total_kg = sum(catch_kg, na.rm = TRUE))
```

## Put it all together

This is the real reward. Using everything from the last two lessons, you can answer a proper question,
like *"how much does each gear bring in?"* You **group by** gear, then **add up**. Press **Run**:

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
landings |>
  group_by(gear) |>
  summarise(
    total_kg = sum(catch_kg, na.rm = TRUE),
    number   = n()
  )
```

### Your turn: your own district

Now answer the question a supervisor actually asks: *"in **my** district, how much does each gear bring
in?"*

That means one more step at the front. **Filter** to your district, **group by** gear, then **add up**.

Replace the blanks `______` with one district name from your own data, keeping the quotes, then press
**Run**. Press **Hint** if you need it.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_summary_district
#| envir: global
#| caption: "Total catch per gear, in your own district"
landings |>
  filter(gaul_2_name == "______") |>
  group_by(gear) |>
  summarise(
    total_kg = sum(catch_kg, na.rm = TRUE),
    number   = n()
  )
```

::: { .hint exercise="ex_summary_district" }
You can see the district names in your own data with `distinct(landings, gaul_2_name)`. Copy one **exactly**
as it is spelled, between the quotes.
:::

::: { .solution exercise="ex_summary_district" }
With a district called `Kilifi` it would be:

```r
landings |>
  filter(gaul_2_name == "Kilifi") |>
  group_by(gear) |>
  summarise(
    total_kg = sum(catch_kg, na.rm = TRUE),
    number   = n()
  )
```
:::

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**What you should see:** one row per fishing method used in that district, with its total weight and how
many catch records there were. That is a real answer to a real question — from your own records.

If the table comes back **empty**, the district name is spelled differently in your data. Check it with
`distinct(landings, gaul_2_name)` and copy it again.
:::

## Now write one from nothing

One last task, and this time there are no blanks to fill. The box below is **empty**. Write the answer
yourself, using the two commands from this lesson.

**The question:** *across all your records, what is the total weight for each kind of fish?*

Take your time. Press **Hint** as often as you need, and **Solution** if you would rather see it and read
it through. Getting there with a hint still counts.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_make_taxon
#| envir: global
#| caption: "Total weight for each kind of fish"
# Write your answer here. Start from landings.

```

::: { .hint exercise="ex_make_taxon" }
Every answer in this lesson had the same three parts. Start from your table, **then** group, **then** add
up:

```r
landings |>
  group_by( ... ) |>
  summarise( ... )
```
:::

::: { .hint exercise="ex_make_taxon" }
The kind of fish is the column `catch_taxon`, and the weight is `catch_kg`. Remember `na.rm = TRUE` so
missing weights are skipped.
:::

::: { .solution exercise="ex_make_taxon" }
```r
landings |>
  group_by(catch_taxon) |>
  summarise(total_kg = sum(catch_kg, na.rm = TRUE))
```
:::

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**What you should see:** one row for each kind of fish in your records, with its total weight. The largest
number is the species that brings in the most weight overall.

Want to go further? Add `filter(gaul_2_name == "...")` as a first step to answer it for **your district
only**.
:::

## What you have learned

- **`summarise(name = sum(column))`** — add a column up into one answer (also `mean()` for the average,
  `n()` for a count).
- **`group_by(column)`** before `summarise()` — get **one answer per group** instead of one overall.
- **`na.rm = TRUE`** — skip missing values so you still get a result.

Put together with `filter` and `select` from the last lesson, you can now answer most everyday questions
about your data: totals and averages, for any group, in any part of your records. That is the whole
toolkit — well done.
